report.summary: Literature suggests diminishing returns after ~3–4 reviewers. SmartBear reported one reviewer finds ~50% of defects, two ~60%, three ~75%, four ~85%, five ~90%. Weller (1993) found two inspectors 86%, three 91%, four 96%. For LLMs, ensemble studies show plateau at 3–5 agents. Budget split: allocate 60–70% to finders, 30–40% to verifiers, but adapt dynamically.
risks: Over-fan-out increases latency, cost and false-positive rate due to LLM bias overlap.
Existing numbers are from human inspection; LLM yield curves may differ and lack robust measurement.
Fixed fan-out wastes budget if defects quickly saturate; adaptive mechanisms need careful tuning.
todos: Pilot Daedalus with a known-defect corpus to map the marginal yield curve of LLM reviewers.
Implement dynamic fan-out: start with 3 finders, measure unique defect discovery rate, expand only if >5% new defects.
Test verifier models (e.g., stronger LLM, majority voting, debate) to filter false positives from finders.

handoff.suggestion: Add an adaptive review fan-out engine that monitors the number of unique defects per additional reviewer. When the incremental yield drops below a threshold (e.g., 10% of previous total), stop adding finders and shift budget to a verifier. Use a consensus mechanism where disagreements are escalated to a higher-capability model. Instrument cost/detection trade-offs per review cycle.

name: q32-scaling-review-fanout
question: At what point does adding more review agents stop finding new defects? What is known about the marginal yield curve of review fan-out, and how should a budget be split between more finders and more verifiers?
